claim: Activating LRRK2 mutations cause Parkinson's disease.
source: Activating LRRK2 mutations cause Parkinson's disease, and pathogenic LRRK2 kinase interferes with ciliogenesis.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field, supported by the citation context of the manuscript.

claim: Pathogenic LRRK2 kinase interferes with ciliogenesis.
source: Activating LRRK2 mutations cause Parkinson's disease, and pathogenic LRRK2 kinase interferes with ciliogenesis.
evidence: This claim is supported by the authors' previous work and the data presented in this manuscript.

claim: Cholinergic interneurons of the dorsal striatum lose their cilia in R1441C LRRK2 mutant mice.
source: Previously, we showed that cholinergic interneurons of the dorsal striatum lose their cilia in R1441C LRRK2 mutant mice (Dhekne et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim references prior published work by the authors.

claim: Cilia loss is seen as early as 10 weeks of age in R1441C LRRK2 mutant mice.
source: Here, we show that cilia loss is seen as early as 10 weeks of age in these mice and also in two other mouse strains carrying the most common human G2019S LRRK2 mutation.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the current study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Cilia loss is seen in two mouse strains carrying the G2019S LRRK2 mutation.
source: Here, we show that cilia loss is seen as early as 10 weeks of age in these mice and also in two other mouse strains carrying the most common human G2019S LRRK2 mutation.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Loss of the PPM1H phosphatase yields the same cilia loss phenotype seen in mice expressing pathogenic LRRK2 kinase.
source: Loss of the PPM1H phosphatase that is specific for LRRK2-phosphorylated Rab GTPases yields the same cilia loss phenotype seen in mice expressing pathogenic LRRK2 kinase, strongly supporting a connection between Rab GTPase phosphorylation and cilia loss.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 5.

claim: PPM1H is specific for LRRK2-phosphorylated Rab GTPases.
source: Loss of the PPM1H phosphatase that is specific for LRRK2-phosphorylated Rab GTPases yields the same cilia loss phenotype seen in mice expressing pathogenic LRRK2 kinase, strongly supporting a connection between Rab GTPase phosphorylation and cilia loss.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Berndsen et al., 2019).

claim: There is a connection between Rab GTPase phosphorylation and cilia loss.
source: Loss of the PPM1H phosphatase that is specific for LRRK2-phosphorylated Rab GTPases yields the same cilia loss phenotype seen in mice expressing pathogenic LRRK2 kinase, strongly supporting a connection between Rab GTPase phosphorylation and cilia loss.
evidence: This is inferred from the genetic evidence that PPM1H loss phenocopies LRRK2 mutation.

claim: Astrocytes throughout the striatum show a ciliation defect in all LRRK2 and PPM1H mutant models examined.
source: Moreover, astrocytes throughout the striatum show a ciliation defect in all LRRK2 and PPM1H mutant models examined.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figures 2, 3, and 5.

claim: Hedgehog signaling requires cilia.
source: Hedgehog signaling requires cilia, and loss of cilia in LRRK2 mutant rodents correlates with dysregulation of Hedgehog signaling as monitored by in situ hybridization of Gli1 and Gdnf transcripts.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by citations in the manuscript.

claim: Loss of cilia in LRRK2 mutant rodents correlates with dysregulation of Hedgehog signaling.
source: Hedgehog signaling requires cilia, and loss of cilia in LRRK2 mutant rodents correlates with dysregulation of Hedgehog signaling as monitored by in situ hybridization of Gli1 and Gdnf transcripts.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figures 6, 7, and 8.

claim: Dopaminergic neurons of the substantia nigra secrete a Hedgehog signal that is sensed in the striatum to trigger neuroprotection.
source: Dopaminergic neurons of the substantia nigra secrete a Hedgehog signal that is sensed in the striatum to trigger neuroprotection; our data support a model in which LRRK2 and PPM1H mutant mice show altered responses to critical Hedgehog signals in the nigrostriatal pathway.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Gonzalez-Reyes et al., 2012).

claim: LRRK2 and PPM1H mutant mice show altered responses to critical Hedgehog signals in the nigrostriatal pathway.
source: Dopaminergic neurons of the substantia nigra secrete a Hedgehog signal that is sensed in the striatum to trigger neuroprotection; our data support a model in which LRRK2 and PPM1H mutant mice show altered responses to critical Hedgehog signals in the nigrostriatal pathway.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Mutations in the LRRK2 gene represent the predominant cause of familial Parkinson's disease.
source: Mutations in the kinase encoded by the LRRK2 gene represent the predominant cause of familial Parkinson's disease (PD), a neurodegenerative disorder that results in the loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta (Poewe et al., 2017; Alessi and Sammler, 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Parkinson's disease is a neurodegenerative disorder that results in the loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta.
source: Mutations in the kinase encoded by the LRRK2 gene represent the predominant cause of familial Parkinson's disease (PD), a neurodegenerative disorder that results in the loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta (Poewe et al., 2017; Alessi and Sammler, 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: A subset of Rab GTPases comprise LRRK2's primary substrates.
source: LRRK2 encodes a protein kinase and recent work has shown that a subset of Rab GTPases comprise its primary substrates (Steger et al., 2016; Steger et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Pathogenic mutations in LRRK2's ROC domain (e.g. R1441C) increase its kinase activity in cells.
source: Pathogenic mutations that localize to LRRK2's ROC domain (e.g. R1441C) and kinase domain (e.g. G2019S) increase its kinase activity in cells (West et al., 2005; Greggio et al., 2006; Jaleel et al., 2007; Ito et al., 2016; Steger et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Pathogenic mutations in LRRK2's kinase domain (e.g. G2019S) increase its kinase activity in cells.
source: Pathogenic mutations that localize to LRRK2's ROC domain (e.g. R1441C) and kinase domain (e.g. G2019S) increase its kinase activity in cells (West et al., 2005; Greggio et al., 2006; Jaleel et al., 2007; Ito et al., 2016; Steger et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Interactions with Rab29 can activate LRRK2.
source: and interactions with other proteins including Rab29 (Kuwahara et al., 2016; Purlyte et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2018; Gomez et al., 2019) and VPS35 can also activate LRRK2 (Linhart et al., 2014; Mir et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Interactions with VPS35 can activate LRRK2.
source: and interactions with other proteins including Rab29 (Kuwahara et al., 2016; Purlyte et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2018; Gomez et al., 2019) and VPS35 can also activate LRRK2 (Linhart et al., 2014; Mir et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Reversal of LRRK2 phosphorylation is mediated at least in part by the PPM1H phosphatase.
source: Reversal of LRRK2 phosphorylation is mediated at least in part by the PPM1H phosphatase that was recently discovered to specifically reverse LRRK2 action on multiple Rab GTPases (Berndsen et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: PPM1H specifically reverses LRRK2 action on multiple Rab GTPases.
source: Reversal of LRRK2 phosphorylation is mediated at least in part by the PPM1H phosphatase that was recently discovered to specifically reverse LRRK2 action on multiple Rab GTPases (Berndsen et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Loss of PPM1H in wild-type mouse embryonic fibroblast cells phenocopies the loss of cilia seen upon expression of pathogenic LRRK2.
source: In cell culture, loss of PPM1H in wild-type mouse embryonic fibroblast (MEF) cells phenocopies the loss of cilia seen upon expression of pathogenic LRRK2 (Berndsen et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Rab GTPases are master regulators of protein trafficking.
source: Rab GTPases are master regulators of protein trafficking and carry out their roles by binding to specific partner proteins when the Rabs are GTP-bound (Pfeffer, 2017; Pfeffer, 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Rab GTPases carry out their roles by binding to specific partner proteins when the Rabs are GTP-bound.
source: Rab GTPases are master regulators of protein trafficking and carry out their roles by binding to specific partner proteins when the Rabs are GTP-bound (Pfeffer, 2017; Pfeffer, 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Phosphorylation of Rab proteins interferes with their abilities to be loaded with GTP by cognate guanine nucleotide exchange factors.
source: Phosphorylation of Rab proteins interferes with their abilities to be loaded with GTP by cognate guanine nucleotide exchange factors, a prerequisite for their binding to partner effector proteins (Steger et al., 2016; Steger et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Once phosphorylated, Rab GTPases switch their preference and bind to new sets of phospho-specific protein effectors.
source: Strikingly, once phosphorylated, Rab GTPases switch their preference and bind to new sets of phospho-specific protein effectors.
evidence: This is supported by the subsequent citations to prior work.

claim: Phospho-specific protein effectors for Rab8 and Rab10 include RILPL1, RILPL2, JIP3, and JIP4 proteins.
source: For Rab8 and Rab10 these include RILPL1, RILPL2, JIP3, and JIP4 proteins (Steger et al., 2017; Dhekne et al., 2018; Waschbüsch et al., 2020) and Myosin Va (Dhekne et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Myosin Va is a phospho-specific protein effector for Rab8 and Rab10.
source: For Rab8 and Rab10 these include RILPL1, RILPL2, JIP3, and JIP4 proteins (Steger et al., 2017; Dhekne et al., 2018; Waschbüsch et al., 2020) and Myosin Va (Dhekne et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: LRRK2 blocks ciliogenesis in cell culture and mouse brain via a process that requires RILPL1 and Rab10 proteins.
source: The consequences of new phospho-Rab interactions include pathways by which LRRK2 blocks ciliogenesis in cell culture and mouse brain via a process that requires RILPL1 and Rab10 proteins (Steger et al., 2017; Dhekne et al., 2018; Sobu et al., 2021)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Centriolar cohesion is altered by LRRK2.
source: centriolar cohesion is also altered (Madero-Pérez et al., 2018; Lara Ordónez et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: LRRK2 is most highly expressed in immune cells, lung, kidney, and intestine.
source: LRRK2 is most highly expressed in immune cells, lung, kidney, and intestine, but it is also present in varying levels throughout the brain (Lis et al., 2018; West et al., 2014; Mandemakers et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: LRRK2 is present in varying levels throughout the brain.
source: LRRK2 is most highly expressed in immune cells, lung, kidney, and intestine, but it is also present in varying levels throughout the brain (Lis et al., 2018; West et al., 2014; Mandemakers et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The striatum is comprised primarily of medium spiny neurons, interneurons and glial cells such as astrocytes.
source: The striatum is comprised primarily of medium spiny neurons, interneurons and glial cells such as astrocytes.
evidence: This is established neuroanatomical knowledge.

claim: Dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra secrete Sonic Hedgehog that is sensed by cholinergic interneurons in the striatum.
source: In an important study, Gonzalez-Reyes et al., 2012 showed that dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra secrete Sonic Hedgehog (Hh) that is sensed by poorly abundant, cholinergic interneurons in the striatum.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Hedgehog is needed for the survival of cholinergic interneurons and dopaminergic neurons.
source: Hh is needed for the survival of both these cholinergic target cells and the Hh-producing dopaminergic neurons, despite the fact that only the cholinergic neurons express the PTCH1 Hh receptor.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Gonzalez-Reyes et al., 2012).

claim: Only cholinergic neurons express the PTCH1 Hh receptor.
source: Hh is needed for the survival of both these cholinergic target cells and the Hh-producing dopaminergic neurons, despite the fact that only the cholinergic neurons express the PTCH1 Hh receptor.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Gonzalez-Reyes et al., 2012).

claim: Hedgehog triggers secretion of glial derived neurotrophic factor (GDNF) from cholinergic neurons.
source: Gonzalez-Reyes et al., 2012 showed further that Hh triggers secretion of glial derived neurotrophic factor (GDNF) from the cholinergic neurons, which provides reciprocal neuroprotection for the dopaminergic neurons of the substantia nigra.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: GDNF provides reciprocal neuroprotection for the dopaminergic neurons of the substantia nigra.
source: Gonzalez-Reyes et al., 2012 showed further that Hh triggers secretion of glial derived neurotrophic factor (GDNF) from the cholinergic neurons, which provides reciprocal neuroprotection for the dopaminergic neurons of the substantia nigra.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Rare, striatal, cholinergic interneurons are less ciliated in mice carrying the R1441C LRRK2 mutation.
source: We found previously that the rare, striatal, cholinergic interneurons that would normally sense Hh via their primary cilia are less ciliated in mice carrying the R1441C LRRK2 mutation (Dhekne et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Cilia loss would decrease the ability of cholinergic interneurons to sense Hh signals.
source: In that study, we proposed that cilia loss would decrease the ability of these cells to sense Hh signals.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed in prior work.

claim: Hedgehog signaling is impacted by cilia loss in multiple LRRK2 mutant mouse models.
source: We show here that Hh signaling is indeed impacted by cilia loss in multiple LRRK2 mutant mouse models.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the current study.

claim: Striatal astrocytes share a broad ciliary deficit in LRRK2 mutant mice.
source: Moreover, we show that striatal astrocytes share a broad ciliary deficit that likely impacts synaptic function.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the current study.

claim: Ciliary deficit in striatal astrocytes likely impacts synaptic function.
source: Moreover, we show that striatal astrocytes share a broad ciliary deficit that likely impacts synaptic function.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the observed ciliary deficit.

claim: Cholinergic interneurons represent about 5% of the neurons in the dorsal striatum.
source: We showed previously that cholinergic interneurons that represent about 5% of the neurons in the dorsal striatum of 7 month, R1441C LRRK2 knock-in (KI) mice have fewer primary cilia than their wild type littermates (Dhekne et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: 7 month R1441C LRRK2 knock-in mice have fewer primary cilia in cholinergic interneurons than their wild type littermates.
source: We showed previously that cholinergic interneurons that represent about 5% of the neurons in the dorsal striatum of 7 month, R1441C LRRK2 knock-in (KI) mice have fewer primary cilia than their wild type littermates (Dhekne et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: G2019S LRRK2 is the most common PD-associated mutation in humans.
source: G2019S LRRK2 is the most common PD-associated mutation in humans, thus it was also important to investigate ciliation in the brains of G2019S LRRK2 mice.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: G2019S LRRK2 is a hyperactive kinase but less active than R1441C LRRK2 when assayed in cell culture.
source: G2019S LRRK2 is a hyperactive kinase but less active than R1441C LRRK2 when assayed in cell culture (cf. Steger et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Mouse cilia lengthen with age.
source: The age of the mice was also important: mouse cilia lengthen with age (Arellano et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: LRRK2 mutations are incompletely penetrant.
source: and LRRK2 mutations are incompletely penetrant, making age an important variable in disease onset (Lee et al., 2017; Domingo and Klein, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Age is an important variable in disease onset for LRRK2 mutations.
source: and LRRK2 mutations are incompletely penetrant, making age an important variable in disease onset (Lee et al., 2017; Domingo and Klein, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: 13 month G2019S LRRK2 KI mice displayed a significant loss of primary cilia in ChAT interneurons of the dorsal striatum.
source: Similar to what we observed previously for 7 month R1441C LRRK2 mice, 13 month G2019S LRRK2 KI mice also displayed a significant loss of primary cilia in choline acetyltransferase (ChAT) interneurons of the dorsal striatum (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 1A and B.

claim: Primary cilia loss in G2019S LRRK2 KI mice was cell-type specific.
source: As before, primary cilia loss was cell-type specific as there was no difference in ciliation or cilia length in the surrounding cells (primarily medium spiny neurons) between mutant and wild-type groups (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: There was no significant difference in cilia length between wild type and G2019S LRRK2 KI cholinergic neurons that retained cilia.
source: For cholinergic neurons that retained cilia, we detected no significant difference in length between wild type and mutant groups (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Cilia length is thought to reflect signaling capacity.
source: Cilia length is important to assess as it is thought to reflect signaling capacity (Guo et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: 10 month G2019S LRRK2 BAC Tg mice displayed a decrease in ciliated cholinergic interneurons.
source: In the brains of the 10 month G2019S LRRK2 BAC Tg mice, we also detected a decrease in ciliated cholinergic interneurons (Figure 1D and E), comparable to that seen in the G2019S KI mice
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 1D and E.

claim: When a primary cilium was present in G2019S LRRK2 BAC Tg mice, it was not significantly shorter than wild type control cells.
source: when a primary cilium was present, it was not significantly shorter than wild type control cells (Figure 1F)
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: G2019S LRRK2 mice have primary cilia defects of the same magnitude as previously observed in cholinergic neurons of the dorsal striatum of R1441C LRRK2 KI mice.
source: Taken together, these data show that G2019S LRRK2 mice have primary cilia defects of the same magnitude as previously observed in cholinergic neurons of the dorsal striatum of R1441C LRRK2 KI mice and cultured cells (Steger et al., 2017; Dhekne et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data presented in the manuscript and comparison to prior work.

claim: G2019S mice did not show defects in cortical ciliogenesis.
source: Unlike the R1441C mice however, G2019S mice did not show defects in cortical ciliogenesis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mouse LRRK2 is more highly expressed in astrocytes than neurons.
source: Mouse LRRK2 is more highly expressed in astrocytes than neurons (Zhang et al., 2014; http://www.brainrnaseq.org)
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work and a database.

claim: Astrocytes in adult mouse brain do not express detectable amounts of AC3.
source: Astrocytic primary cilia were detected using antibodies specific for ADP Ribosylation Factor Like GTPase 13B (Arl13B) because astrocytes in adult mouse brain do not express detectable amounts of Adenylate Cyclase three (AC3) that we use to stain cilia in neurons (Dhekne et al., 2018; Sterpka and Chen, 2018; Sipos et al., 2018; Kasahara et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: GFAP+ G2019S LRRK2 KI astrocytes in the dorsal striatum were less likely to have Arl13B+ primary cilia relative to wild type controls.
source: Strikingly, we found that GFAP+ G2019S LRRK2 KI and G2019S BAC Tg astrocytes in the dorsal striatum were less likely to have Arl13B+ primary cilia relative to wild type controls (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 2.

claim: GFAP+ G2019S BAC Tg astrocytes in the dorsal striatum were less likely to have Arl13B+ primary cilia relative to wild type controls.
source: Strikingly, we found that GFAP+ G2019S LRRK2 KI and G2019S BAC Tg astrocytes in the dorsal striatum were less likely to have Arl13B+ primary cilia relative to wild type controls (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The remaining GFAP+ cilia in the G2019S BAC Tg astrocytes were very slightly but significantly shorter.
source: In addition, the remaining GFAP+ cilia in the G2019S BAC Tg astrocytes were very slightly but significantly shorter (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Striatal astrocytes from G2019S LRRK2 KI mice have fewer primary cilia.
source: Thus, GFAP+ striatal astrocytes from G2019S LRRK2 KI mice have fewer primary cilia, and striatal astrocytes also have shorter primary cilia upon pathogenic LRRK2 overexpression.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Striatal astrocytes have shorter primary cilia upon pathogenic LRRK2 overexpression.
source: Thus, GFAP+ striatal astrocytes from G2019S LRRK2 KI mice have fewer primary cilia, and striatal astrocytes also have shorter primary cilia upon pathogenic LRRK2 overexpression.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Astrocyte cilia were shorter overall compared with neuronal cilia.
source: Note that astrocyte cilia were shorter overall compared with neuronal cilia (Figures 1C, F, 2C and F), and all cilia were shorter in the BAC Tg mice.
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in the indicated figures.

claim: All cilia were shorter in the BAC Tg mice.
source: Note that astrocyte cilia were shorter overall compared with neuronal cilia (Figures 1C, F, 2C and F), and all cilia were shorter in the BAC Tg mice.
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in the indicated figures.

claim: Primary cilia loss in cholinergic interneurons of the dorsal striatum could be detected as early as 10 weeks of age in R1441C LRRK2 KI mice.
source: As shown in Figure 3A and B, primary cilia loss in cholinergic interneurons of the dorsal striatum could be detected as early as 10 weeks of age in R1441C LRRK2 KI mice; note that these were the youngest animals analyzed.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: At 10 weeks of age, fewer striatal cholinergic interneurons have a primary cilium (~40%) in R1441C LRRK2 mice in comparison with their non-transgenic littermates (~60%).
source: At this age, fewer striatal cholinergic interneurons have a primary cilium (~40%) in comparison with their non-transgenic littermates (~60%; Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Overall neuronal ciliation in the dorsal striatum in 10 week wild type and R1441C mutant groups was slightly lower but similar to the overall values seen previously in a 7 month R1441C LRRK2 KI cohort (~70%).
source: Overall neuronal ciliation in the dorsal striatum in 10 week wild type and R1441C mutant groups was slightly lower but similar to the overall values seen previously in a 7 month R1441C LRRK2 KI cohort (~70%; Dhekne et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a comparison to prior work.

claim: 2 weeks of MLi-2 feeding did not alter the extent of ciliation or cilia length in cholinergic interneurons in R1441C LRRK2 mice.
source: As shown in Figure 3A, C and D, 2 weeks of MLi-2 feeding did not alter the extent of ciliation or cilia length in cholinergic interneurons or astrocytes in the LRRK2 R1441C mice.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 3A, C and D.

claim: 2 weeks of MLi-2 feeding did not alter the extent of ciliation or cilia length in astrocytes in R1441C LRRK2 mice.
source: As shown in Figure 3A, C and D, 2 weeks of MLi-2 feeding did not alter the extent of ciliation or cilia length in cholinergic interneurons or astrocytes in the LRRK2 R1441C mice.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 3A, C and D.

claim: Despite 2 weeks of MLi-2 administration, there was no significant difference in ciliation or cilia length for GFAP and S100B positive astrocytes or S100B only positive astrocytes upon treatment.
source: We also scored primary cilia in two distinct populations of astrocytes – cells that were positive for both GFAP and S100B, and those that were only positive for S100B (Figure 3E–G). Despite 2 weeks of MLi-2 administration, we failed to detect a significant difference in ciliation or cilia length for either population of astrocytes upon treatment.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 3E–G.

claim: Neurons and astrocytes are postmitotic cells with much less dynamic cilia than dividing cells.
source: It is important to note that neurons and astrocytes are postmitotic cells with much less dynamic cilia than dividing cells (Sterpka and Chen, 2018)
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Longer times of drug treatment may be needed to reveal an effect of MLi-2 on ciliation in neurons and astrocytes.
source: longer times of drug treatment may very well be needed to reveal an effect.
evidence: This is speculation based on the lack of effect observed with 2 weeks of treatment.

claim: LRRK2 inhibitors decrease LRRK2 phosphorylation at serine 935.
source: LRRK2 inhibitors decrease LRRK2 phosphorylation at serine 935 (cf. Fell et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: pS935-LRRK2 was diminished in wild-type and R1441C LRRK2 brains from mice fed MLi-2 inhibitor.
source: and pS935-LRRK2 was diminished in wild-type and R1441C LRRK2 brains from mice fed MLi-2 inhibitor, consistent with inhibitor access in this tissue.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: Rab12 S105 phosphorylation decreased in wild type and mutant brain upon MLi-2 treatment.
source: Rab12 S105 phosphorylation also decreased in wild type (Figure 4C) and mutant (Figure 4A and B) brain.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 4A, B, and C.

claim: Levels of pRab10 seemed unchanged with MLi-2 treatment with variability among animals.
source: However, levels of pRab10 seemed unchanged (Figure 4A and B) with variability among animals (see also Iannotta et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: MLi-2 administration does not markedly reduce pRab10 levels in brain.
source: Previous studies have also noted that MLi-2 administration does not markedly reduce pRab10 levels in brain (Kelly et al., 2018; Kalogeropulou et al., 2020; Nirujogi et al., 2021; Kluss et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Analysis of whole brain will not capture the precise status of pRab10 levels in rare cholinergic neurons of the dorsal striatum that show LRRK2 mutation-associated ciliary deficits.
source: Note that analysis of whole brain in this experiment will not capture the precise status of pRab10 levels in rare cholinergic neurons of the dorsal striatum that show LRRK2 mutation-associated ciliary deficits.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the limitations of the experimental approach.

claim: The available anti-phosphoRab10 antibody cannot be used for tissue immunohistochemistry at a single-cell level.
source: Unfortunately, the available anti-phosphoRab10 antibody cannot be used for tissue immunohistochemistry at a single-cell level.
evidence: This is a statement about a technical limitation.

claim: Even heterozygous loss of PPM1H leads to decreased cilia numbers in cholinergic interneurons of the dorsal striatum of 5.5 month-old mice.
source: Figure 5 shows that even heterozygous loss of PPM1H leads to decreased cilia numbers in cholinergic interneurons (Figure 5A and B) and astrocytes (Figure 5C and D) of the dorsal striatum of 5.5 month-old mice.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: Even heterozygous loss of PPM1H leads to decreased cilia numbers in astrocytes of the dorsal striatum of 5.5 month-old mice.
source: Figure 5 shows that even heterozygous loss of PPM1H leads to decreased cilia numbers in cholinergic interneurons (Figure 5A and B) and astrocytes (Figure 5C and D) of the dorsal striatum of 5.5 month-old mice.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 5C and D.

claim: Analysis of 2.5 month-old homozygous PPM1H knockout mice showed a slightly greater defect in ciliation of cholinergic interneurons.
source: Analysis of 2.5 month-old homozygous PPM1H knockout mice showed a slightly greater defect, despite the fact that fewer cholinergic neurons were ciliated at this age (compare Figure 5B left and right panels).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: High PPM1H levels in wild type brain are important to counteract LRRK2 action.
source: These data demonstrate the importance of high PPM1H levels in wild type brain to counteract LRRK2 action.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the PPM1H knockout data.

claim: Loss of the phosphatase PPM1H shows the same phenotype as the presence of a hyperactive LRRK2 mutation, validating a link between LRRK2-Rab phosphorylation and ciliogenesis in specific brain cell types.
source: More importantly, they strongly validate a link between LRRK2-Rab phosphorylation and ciliogenesis in specific brain cell types because loss of the phosphatase shows the same phenotype as the presence of a hyperactive LRRK2 mutation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the PPM1H knockout data.

claim: Immunoblotting showed an appropriate reduction of PPM1H protein levels in brain extracts from Ppm1h-/+ and Ppm1h-/- mice.

claim: Loss of Hedgehog production by dopaminergic neurons decreases Gdnf transcripts and protein levels in the striatum in an age-dependent manner.

claim: Most GDNF was expressed by cholinergic neurons (and not surrounding cells) in the dorsal striatum of wild type mice.

claim: Loss of Gli3 repression in non-ciliated LRRK2 mutant neurons may increase GDNF production in those cells.

It is possible that loss of Gli3 repression in non-ciliated LRRK2 mutant neurons increases GDNF production in those cells.
